title: Short Stuff: MacGuffins
summary: Short Stuff episode in which Josh and Chuck (with Jerry sitting in) try to pin down what a MacGuffin is in film and fiction. They debate the two competing definitions, the Maltese Falcon, Raiders of the Lost Ark, The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, Hitchcock's use of the term, and its origin, including Angus MacPhail's tiger story and the Pearl White "weenie" serials. They close with more examples such as R2-D2 in Star Wars, Escape from New York's cassette tape, and the briefcase in Pulp Fiction, and ask listeners who are film students or cinephiles for a clearer definition.

segments.title: Opening banter and the question of what a MacGuffin is
segments.summary: Josh introduces the short stuff as a question that will probably never be answered: what is a MacGuffin? He describes it as a plot device that moves the story and motivates characters, and the hosts agree the definitions differ on its role.

segments.title: Competing definitions and the Maltese Falcon and Raiders examples
segments.summary: Chuck cites the Maltese Falcon as the classic example, the statuette everyone chases. Josh explains the two definitions: one says the object drives the whole plot, the other says it matters to characters but is unimportant to the overall plot. Chuck gives Raiders of the Lost Ark's gold head and says George Lucas considered the Ark of the Covenant a MacGuffin. The hosts debate whether the Ark's power would still make it one.

segments.title: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd and the blackmail letter
segments.summary: Josh offers a new example from Agatha Christie's The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, where the murderer wants a blackmail letter, which matters to the characters but not to the overall investigation. Chuck agrees it seems like a MacGuffin. Josh says he cannot grasp why some things are labeled MacGuffins and others are not.

segments.title: Hitchcock's explanations and the Psycho and origin stories
segments.summary: Chuck explains Hitchcock popularized the term and gave several explanations, including the spies' goal the audience does not care about. Chuck contrasts this with George Lucas's view of R2-D2 in Star Wars. Hosts discuss North by Northwest and Psycho, where Janet Leigh's stolen forty grand sets the plot in motion. Chuck covers the word's origin: possibly from 'guff' or from Angus MacPhail's Scottish train story about tiger hunting in Scotland.

segments.title: Pearl White and the weenie serials
segments.summary: Josh says the concept predates Hitchcock. Citing TV Tropes, he describes silent film actress Pearl White's cliffhanger serials, which were built around chasing an object and which she called weenies. The hosts agree they like the term weenie.

segments.title: More film examples and closing call to listeners
segments.summary: Chuck names the cassette tape in Escape from New York, which is never heard. Josh mentions a Wilford Brimley John Carpenter movie as a MacGuffin. Josh cites R2-D2 and the Pulp Fiction briefcase, which is never explained. The hosts briefly digress on Tarantino, then ask film students and cinephiles to help give a clearer definition.

segments.title: Sign-off and production credit
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the short stuff and the episode ends with the standard iHeartRadio production credit.
